sources.title: Electromyographic Analysis of Latissimus Dorsi Activation During Common Resistance Training Exercises: A Narrative Review

grip width findings inconsistent
narrower seated-row grip and lower shoulder-abduction angle each supported independently in separate studies
pull-up grips broadly similar in available evidence
pullover did not selectively favor lats in available evidence
limitations: EMG is acute muscle activation, not longitudinal hypertrophy
findings are tentative; some comparisons come from small studies

narrow/medium grip allowed slightly more 6RM load than wide grip in this sample

acute EMG and performance test, not long-term growth

three specific variants only
not a hypertrophy trial

acute loading/EMG, not hypertrophy

exercises.name: Lat Pulldown
exercises.finding: Front-of-body pulldown has the most consistent lat-EMG support in the recent review; grip width alone is not a reliable universal winner.
limitations: EMG does not establish long-term hypertrophy superiority
exercises.nerdFact: The bar path and how your elbows travel can change which pulling muscles do more of the work. Use a grip you can control and progress rather than chasing an extra-wide grip.

exercises.name: Pull-up
exercises.finding: Strong bodyweight vertical pull; tested grip/device variants generally produced similar lat EMG.
limitations: may be too difficult for some users; offer assisted variant
exercises.nerdFact: Pull-ups train your lats along with your arms and other back muscles. Different grips can work well, so choose one you can perform with control.

exercises.name: Assisted Pull-up
exercises.finding: Makes the vertical-pull pattern scalable for users who cannot yet complete strict pull-ups.
limitations: assistance step size and machine mechanics vary
exercises.nerdFact: The assistance lets you train the pull-up pattern before you can lift your full bodyweight. Reduce assistance gradually as your strength improves.

exercises.name: One-Arm Cable Pulldown
exercises.finding: Strong practical option with adjustable line of pull and unilateral training flexibility.
limitations: not established as more hypertrophic than bilateral pulldowns
exercises.nerdFact: Using one arm lets you adjust the cable path to a comfortable position. The main benefit is flexibility, not a guarantee of extra growth.

exercises.name: Seated Cable Row
exercises.finding: Versatile row; the arm path and elbow position change emphasis. Separate studies suggest closer grip and lower shoulder-abduction angle can increase lat EMG, but this exact combination has not been validated together.
limitations: multiple muscles work together; avoid claims of isolation
exercises.nerdFact: Rows train several back muscles at once. A repeatable, controlled pulling path makes it easier to track your progress.

exercises.name: Chest-Supported Row
exercises.finding: A stable rowing choice with good progression practicality; recommendation is based mostly on exercise mechanics and programming utility, not proof of unique hypertrophy superiority.
limitations: specific machines and elbow paths differ
exercises.nerdFact: The chest pad supports your torso, so you can focus on the pull without having to hold yourself bent over.

exercises.name: Machine Row
exercises.finding: Good practical option when the machine's path feels comfortable and can be progressed reliably.
limitations: machine geometry varies; no universal best machine path
exercises.nerdFact: A machine row guides the movement and can make it easier to repeat the same setup from workout to workout.

exercises.name: One-Arm Cable Row
exercises.finding: Flexible row for adjusting the pull path and training one side at a time.
limitations: unilateral work is not inherently superior for hypertrophy
exercises.nerdFact: A one-arm row makes it easy to adjust your elbow path and work each side separately. Pick the version you can control and progress.

exercises.name: One-Arm Dumbbell Row
exercises.finding: Useful free-weight row; support and torso position strongly affect the practical demand.
limitations: specific lat/upper-back emphasis depends on execution
exercises.nerdFact: You can change the angle of a one-arm dumbbell row to suit your target. Keep the setup consistent so your progress is easy to compare.

exercises.name: T-Bar Row
exercises.finding: A loadable row that can emphasize lats or upper back depending on grip, torso and elbow path.
limitations: supported and unsupported versions differ meaningfully
exercises.nerdFact: T-bar rows can train the lats and upper back together. Your handle and elbow path change which area gets more emphasis.

exercises.name: Barbell Row
exercises.finding: Strong compound row; unsupported torso position increases trunk stabilization and can increase lumbar loading relative to some supported options.
limitations: not automatically the best option for everyone or every target
exercises.nerdFact: Barbell rows train the lats and upper back while your trunk works to hold your position. Supported rows are another good choice when you want less lower-back demand.

exercises.name: Inverted Row
exercises.finding: Scalable bodyweight row; one small acute comparison found high lat/upper-back activation and lower lumbar loading among the three tested row variations.
limitations: single small acute study; do not rank universally first from it
exercises.nerdFact: Inverted rows use your bodyweight instead of a cable or barbell load. Raising or lowering the body angle can make the exercise easier or harder.

exercises.name: Straight-Arm Pulldown
exercises.finding: Reasonable shoulder-extension accessory, but not proven to be the best or an isolating lat hypertrophy movement.
limitations: direct hypertrophy comparisons limited
exercises.nerdFact: This variation lets you pull through the shoulder with relatively little elbow bending. It can complement rows and pulldowns rather than replace them.

exercises.name: Dumbbell Pullover
exercises.finding: Keep selectable if present, but do not automatically rank as a top lat movement; available EMG evidence did not show selective lat emphasis.
limitations: muscle contribution depends on technique and is not fully resolved by acute EMG
exercises.nerdFact: Pullovers can involve both chest and back muscles. How you perform the movement affects which muscles contribute most.

exercises.name: Reverse Pec Deck
exercises.finding: Strong practical rear-delt movement with upper-back contribution; not a substitute for rowing when the priority is overall upper-back mass.
limitations: primary target is rear deltoid, not all upper-back muscles equally
exercises.nerdFact: The reverse pec deck mainly trains the back of your shoulders, with upper-back muscles helping control the movement.

exercises.name: Reverse Fly
exercises.finding: Useful rear-delt-focused accessory; upper-back recruitment varies with execution.
limitations: not equivalent to a heavy row for general upper-back progression
exercises.nerdFact: Reverse flies mainly train the back of your shoulders. They complement rows by adding a different movement pattern.

exercises.name: Face Pull
exercises.finding: Useful accessory for rear shoulders and scapular musculature; not the default primary mass-building row.
limitations: exercise execution varies; evidence is mainly activation/rehab-oriented
exercises.nerdFact: Face pulls combine a pull with an outward rotation of the arms. They are often used as an accessory for the rear shoulders and upper back.

exercises.name: Dumbbell Shrug
exercises.finding: A strong target-specific candidate for upper traps; tested shrug EMG supports the movement pattern, not a unique superiority of dumbbells.
limitations: no direct evidence proving dumbbells outperform barbell/cable/machine shrugs for growth
exercises.nerdFact: Shrugs directly train the upper traps, which help lift your shoulder blades. Dumbbell, barbell, cable and machine versions can all be useful.

exercises.name: Barbell Shrug
exercises.finding: Loadable shrug option; use comfort, available equipment and repeatable progression to distinguish from other shrug versions.
limitations: no universal best implement established
exercises.nerdFact: Barbell shrugs let you progressively load the upper traps. Choose a comfortable setup and keep the movement controlled.

exercises.name: Machine Shrug
exercises.finding: A practical stable shrug choice when the machine fits the user and supports smooth progression.
limitations: machine designs vary; comparative hypertrophy evidence limited
exercises.nerdFact: A shrug machine guides the movement and makes it easy to repeat your setup. Its value comes from comfortable, progressive training.

exercises.name: Cable Shrug
exercises.finding: Practical shrug alternative; resistance feel and setup depend on cable position.
limitations: no evidence of universal superiority over other shrug types
exercises.nerdFact: Cable shrugs provide another way to train the upper traps. Pick the setup that feels comfortable and lets you increase the load over time.

exercises.name: Prone Y Raise
exercises.finding: Useful lower-trap-focused accessory; acute EMG evidence does not establish superior lower-trap hypertrophy.
limitations: loads are often light; direct hypertrophy evidence sparse
exercises.nerdFact: The Y-shaped arm path is often used to target the lower traps. Research mainly compares short-term muscle activity, so it is best viewed as a targeted accessory.

exercises.name: Incline Y Raise
exercises.finding: Practical variation for lower-trap emphasis; direct hypertrophy comparison evidence is limited.
limitations: not a main general-back mass movement
exercises.nerdFact: Doing a Y raise on an incline bench supports your body while you move your arms overhead. Use a load you can control without swinging.

exercises.name: Cable Y Raise
exercises.finding: Provides adjustable cable resistance for a lower-trap-focused movement; direct hypertrophy comparisons limited.
limitations: setup may be less intuitive and evidence is not proof of superior growth
exercises.nerdFact: Cable Y raises let you adjust the resistance path. Keep the motion smooth and use a load that you can control.

exercises.name: Prone Cobra
exercises.finding: Acute EMG study found modified prone cobra useful for lower-trap recruitment; direct hypertrophy superiority not established.
limitations: usually limited external loading; more targeted accessory than main mass exercise
exercises.nerdFact: The prone cobra is a light body-position exercise used to train the muscles around the shoulder blades. It is usually an accessory rather than a heavy back exercise.

exercises.name: 45-Degree Back Extension
exercises.finding: Useful targeted extension candidate; how much the movement uses hip extension versus spinal extension affects which muscles are trained.
limitations: small older training trials measured strength/endurance, not hypertrophy; results were mixed for strength
exercises.nerdFact: Back extensions can train your lower-back muscles, glutes and hamstrings. The way you move—more through the spine or more through the hips—changes the emphasis.

exercises.name: Machine Back Extension
exercises.finding: A standardized loaded trunk-extension option when available; the broader exercise family has endurance/strength evidence but little direct hypertrophy evidence.
limitations: machine designs and trunk range vary; confirm existing library entry/equipment
exercises.nerdFact: A back-extension machine guides the trunk movement and can make it easier to use a repeatable range of motion.

exercises.name: Romanian Deadlift
exercises.finding: A compound hip hinge for hamstrings and glutes with the spinal erectors stabilizing the trunk; not an erector isolation exercise.
limitations: the cited source is broad resistance-training evidence, not a head-to-head back hypertrophy study
exercises.nerdFact: Romanian deadlifts mainly train your hamstrings and glutes while your lower-back muscles help keep your torso steady.

exercises.name: Deadlift
exercises.finding: Useful whole-body strength and posterior-chain lift; the trunk and upper back contribute, but it should not automatically be treated as the best pure back hypertrophy exercise.
limitations: high skill and fatigue demands; no exercise-specific hypertrophy superiority established in this pack
exercises.nerdFact: Deadlifts train much of the posterior chain while your back muscles help hold the trunk steady. They are a demanding compound lift, not a back-isolation exercise.

exercises.name: Good Morning
exercises.finding: Advanced hip-hinge movement with significant trunk stabilization demands; should not be a default beginner recommendation.
limitations: not directly ranked against other hinges for back hypertrophy in this evidence pack
exercises.nerdFact: Good mornings train the hamstrings and glutes while your back holds the torso position. Start conservatively and learn the movement before adding substantial load.

rankingGuardrails: Do not use EMG as a direct proxy for hypertrophy.
Do not describe wide-grip pulldowns as universally best for lats.
Do not claim a single row isolates rhomboids or middle traps.
Treat lower-trap Y/cobra movements as targeted accessories, not proven best hypertrophy exercises.
Treat Romanian deadlift and deadlift as compound posterior-chain options, not erector isolation.
Use evidence as one input alongside target fit, goal, priority, equipment, stability, progressability, skill demand and fatigue demand.
Preserve all valid selectable exercise options; only true constraints can filter eligibility.
Before import, match by existing exercise ID/name and avoid duplicates.
Do not mutate existing personal splits, histories or Firebase user data during import.
